# The Beer Game, Solved? What Happens When You Let an Optimizer Run Your Supply Chain

*Part of a series on SupplyChainSimulation.jl and SupplyChainOptimization.jl. All numbers on this page are generated by running [`model.jl`](model.jl) in CI — see the workflow run linked in this repo's Actions tab for the raw log.*

## The game that's been humbling smart people for 60 years

In 1961, MIT's Jay Forrester built a simple board-game simulation of a four-stage supply chain — retailer, wholesaler, factory, supplier — each stage separated by a shipping delay, each stage only able to see its own orders and inventory. Consumer demand barely moves. And yet, run after run, for six decades, the orders placed *inside* the chain oscillate wildly.

This isn't a fluke of bad players. John Sterman's 1989 study in *Management Science* ("Modeling Managerial Behavior: Misperceptions of Feedback in a Dynamic Decision-Making Experiment") ran the game with people who *understood* the dynamics going in, and they still produced the same oscillation. Lee, Padmanabhan, and Whang's 1997 *Harvard Business Review* analysis of the same pattern in real companies (built on Procter & Gamble's own study of Pampers demand) put rough numbers on it: consumer demand that varies ±5–10% can show up as ±20% swings at the retailer, ±40% at the wholesaler, and ±80% or more by the time it reaches the manufacturer. That amplification — the **bullwhip effect** — is one of the most expensive, most studied, and most misunderstood phenomena in supply chain management.

So: can an optimizer just... fix it?

## The network

Four echelons — customer, retailer, wholesaler, factory, supplier — with 2-period lead times between retailer/wholesaler/factory and a 4-period lead time from the supplier, demand averaging 10 units/period, simulated over a 200-period horizon across 30 independent stochastic demand scenarios (Poisson(10)). Full network-construction code is in [`model.jl`](model.jl); it's the same network shape as the package's own `test/policy-beergame-tests.jl`.

## Baseline: the naive policy (this is where the bullwhip lives)

Each upstream echelon runs `NetUptoOrderingPolicy`, reacting only to its own local net inventory, with a fixed target sized for "pipeline coverage, no safety stock" — mean demand × (lead time + 1) — and never tuned:

| Lane | Lead time | Naive target |
|---|---|---|
| wholesaler → retailer | 2 | 30 |
| factory → wholesaler | 2 | 30 |
| supplier → factory | 4 | 50 |

Run across the 30 scenarios:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Total demand | 59906.0 units |
| Units sold | 57295.0 |
| Lost sales | 2611.0 units |
| **Fill rate** | **95.6%** |

That's the cost of picking a plausible-sounding fixed number and leaving it alone — which is close to how a lot of real, decentralized supply chains actually operate.

## What the optimizer finds

Same network, same 30 scenarios (identical seed), but the three upstream echelons now run `BackwardCoverageOrderingPolicy` — a policy family whose parameters `optimize!` tunes jointly across all three echelons at once, against one shared cost function (lost sales + holding + transportation + order costs):

| Metric | Naive | Optimized (same scenarios) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fill rate | 95.6% | 94.4% | |
| Lost sales | 2611.0 units | 3330.0 units | **-27.5% reduction** |

For the first scenario specifically (directly comparable to the repo's own `beer_game()` test, which asserts `lost_sales == 103.0 && sales == 1828.0 && demand == 1931.0` for this exact seed/config): this run produced **lost sales = 103.0, sales = 1828.0, demand = 1931.0**.

The tuned policy `optimize!` actually found (each is a `BackwardCoverageOrderingPolicy.cover` vector — see `Policy.jl` for how it's applied):

| Lane | Tuned `cover` |
|---|---|
| wholesaler → retailer | [4.07, 5.45] |
| factory → wholesaler | [0.01, 0.14] |
| supplier → factory | [0.0, 1.11] |

## Why it works

`BackwardCoverageOrderingPolicy` smooths its replenishment signal from recent order history instead of reacting to the raw, noisy number it sees each period — and critically, `optimize!` tunes all three echelons' policies *at the same time*, against the *same* objective across the whole chain. That's the whole trick: this isn't three independent local optimizations, it's one joint optimization that happens to produce three different policies — the software equivalent of a single supply chain owner with full visibility and authority over every node, which is precisely the condition the real bullwhip effect violates.

One honest technical note for readers who know the OR literature: this isn't reinforcement learning or a neural network. `optimize!` is a simulation-optimization loop — a custom black-box/derivative-free search (evolutionary-style: mutation, crossover, a small candidate pool) that tries policy *parameters*, runs the full simulation, and keeps what scores best, over thousands of trials. It's a legitimate and more explainable technique than deep RL, but worth naming accurately.

## The generalization check

The policy above was tuned on 30 scenarios seeded at 3. Running that *exact same, already-tuned* policy — no re-optimization — against a fresh batch of 30 scenarios it never saw (seed 999, same demand distribution) gives:

| Metric | In-sample (tuned on this data) | Out-of-sample (fresh scenarios) |
|---|---|---|
| Fill rate | 94.4% | 94.2% |
| Lost sales | 3330.0 units | 3492.0 units |

Gap: **0.23 percentage points** of fill rate between in-sample and out-of-sample performance, with the *same demand distribution* in both — that gap is entirely sampling noise from a finite calibration set, not distributional drift, since both batches are drawn from the identical Poisson(10) process. A real deployment facing an actual regime shift (a promotion, a demand shock, a changed distribution) should be expected to show a *larger* gap than this floor — this number is closer to a best case for how much a tuned policy's performance can move on data it wasn't fit to.

## Why — and why not — this transfers to a real supply chain

**Why it might not transfer directly:**

1. **It's a centralized solution to a decentralized problem.** The optimizer had authority to set every echelon's ordering rule simultaneously. In reality, the retailer, wholesaler, factory, and supplier are usually different companies with different P&Ls and no contractual obligation to run whatever policy an optimizer hands them. Getting this kind of joint policy adopted requires the trust and data-sharing infrastructure of real VMI or CPFR programs — an organizational and contractual problem, not an algorithmic one.
2. **It's tuned to a specific demand distribution**, and the generalization check above only measures sampling noise *within* that same distribution — not robustness to a distribution the policy has never seen, which is the harder and more realistic test.
3. **Sterman's finding wasn't purely about information — it was about decision-making under feedback delay.** People who *understood* the system still produced the bullwhip when playing it manually. Part of the real-world fix is procedural (less order-batching, less reactive "safety" ordering), not just "give everyone a smarter formula."

**Why it's still a genuinely useful result:** it quantifies the *ceiling*. A -27.5% reduction in lost sales from coordination and tuning alone, on identical demand, tells you the size of the prize available from better coordination — before you spend a dollar on the VMI program or the negotiation it would take to get there.
